questions.stem: Which group of animals makes up the great apes?
options: Baboons, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans
Lemurs, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos
Orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos and humans
Gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos
questions.explanation: Humans are classified with orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos as great apes (the family Hominidae). Gibbons are lesser apes, baboons are monkeys, and lemurs are more distantly related primates.

questions.stem: Which set of features is shared by primates, including humans?
options: Wings for gliding, a keen sense of smell, and no ability to grasp
Forward-facing eyes, grasping hands with nails, and large brains
Eyes on the sides of the head, hooves on the feet, and a small brain
Claws on every digit, a long snout, and many offspring in each litter
questions.explanation: Primates have forward-facing eyes giving stereoscopic vision, grasping hands and often feet with flat nails, and large brains relative to body size. Many of these features suit life in trees.

questions.stem: What does the term hominin refer to?
options: All of the great apes, including orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and humans
All primates that live mainly on the ground rather than in trees
Any primate that uses tools, including chimpanzees and some monkeys
Humans and extinct species closer to humans than to chimpanzees
questions.explanation: Hominins are the human lineage after it split from the line leading to chimpanzees, including Australopithecus, Paranthropus and Homo. The wider family of great apes is the hominids.

questions.stem: Humans have 46 chromosomes, while the other great apes have 48. Which explanation is supported by DNA evidence?
options: Humans lost two chromosomes, together with all of their genes
The other great apes gained two extra chromosomes from viruses
Humans and apes do not share genes, so they cannot be compared
Two ancestral chromosomes fused to form human chromosome 2
questions.explanation: Human chromosome 2 has banding patterns and DNA sequences matching two separate chromosomes in chimpanzees, along with the remains of an extra centromere and of chromosome ends in its middle. This indicates a fusion in the human lineage.

questions.stem: Humans and chimpanzees share roughly 98 to 99 per cent of their DNA sequence, yet differ greatly in appearance and behaviour. How can such a small difference matter so much?
options: Differences in appearance are caused by the environment alone, so DNA plays no part in them
Chimpanzee DNA is made of different nucleotides, so even matching sequences produce other proteins
Some differ in genes, or in sequences controlling gene expression in development
The shared DNA is not used at all, so only the differing one or two per cent has any effect on the body
questions.explanation: Small differences in key genes, and in regions that regulate gene expression during development, can have large effects, for example on brain growth or skeletal shape. Both species use the same four nucleotides and the same genetic code.

questions.stem: How does the human brain compare with that of a chimpanzee?
options: The human brain is about three times larger, with more cortex
The human brain is about the same size, but has a smaller cerebral cortex
The human brain is smaller, but its cerebellum is much more developed
The human brain is about ten times larger, but its cortex is the same size
questions.explanation: An average adult human brain is roughly three times the volume of a chimpanzee's, and the cerebral cortex, particularly the frontal region, is greatly expanded. This is linked to complex language, planning and culture.

questions.stem: Why is the cerebral cortex of humans highly folded?
options: Folding reduces its surface area so that the brain uses less energy
Folding lets the cortex expand outward through openings in the skull
Folding is caused by pressure from the jaw muscles during chewing
Folding increases its area so more neurons fit inside the skull
questions.explanation: The folds allow a large area of cortex, containing many neurons, to fit within the skull. The greater relative size of the cortex in humans is associated with higher cognitive abilities.

questions.stem: Which skull features of a modern human reflect the large size of the cerebral cortex?
options: A low, sloping cranium with a pronounced brow ridge
A sagittal crest along the top of a small cranium
A long, projecting face with a forward-set jaw
A high, rounded cranium with a near-vertical forehead
questions.explanation: The expanded cerebral cortex, especially the frontal lobes, is housed in a high, domed cranium with a vertical forehead. A low sloping cranium, large brow ridges and a sagittal crest are features of apes and some earlier hominins.

questions.stem: What is a precision grip?
options: Gripping an object between the big toe and the second toe
Holding a small object between thumb and fingertips
Wrapping the whole hand around an object, such as a branch
Hooking the fingers over an object without using the thumb
questions.explanation: A precision grip uses the pads of the thumb and fingertips to hold and manipulate small objects, such as a pen. Wrapping the hand around an object is a power grip.

questions.stem: Which features of the human hand allow a strong precision grip?
options: Claws on each digit and a thumb fused to the index finger
A thumb that cannot rotate and fingers longer than the forearm
A long, fully opposable thumb and relatively short, straight fingers
A short thumb and long, curved fingers suited to hanging from branches
questions.explanation: The long human thumb can rotate to meet the tip of each finger, and the shorter fingers make this easy. Great apes have shorter thumbs and long, curved fingers, which suit climbing and suspension.

questions.stem: How does the big toe of a human differ from that of a chimpanzee?
options: The human big toe has a claw, while the chimpanzee's has a flat nail
The human big toe is in line with the other toes and is not opposable
The human big toe is opposable and can grasp objects like a thumb
The human big toe is shorter than the other toes and points sideways
questions.explanation: In humans the big toe lies parallel to the other toes and helps push off when walking. Chimpanzees and other apes have an opposable big toe that grasps branches.

questions.stem: A fossil foot has an opposable big toe and no arches, while its leg bones show some features of upright walking. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: It may have walked upright on the ground but still climbed trees
The species was fully adapted to long-distance walking, just like modern humans
The species could not have walked upright, because it had an opposable big toe
The species must have walked on its knuckles, because its foot lacked arches
questions.explanation: A grasping toe suggests climbing, while the leg bones suggest some bipedalism, so the species probably combined both. Mixed evidence like this is common in early hominins.

questions.stem: What is bipedalism?
options: Habitually walking upright on two legs
Walking on all four limbs with knuckles down
Swinging arm over arm beneath branches
Climbing trees using hands and feet together
questions.explanation: Bipedalism is the habitual use of two legs for standing and walking. Knuckle-walking is a form of quadrupedalism, and swinging arm over arm is brachiation.

questions.stem: Where is the foramen magnum positioned in a human skull, and why?
options: At the front, so the spinal cord can reach the face more directly
Centrally underneath, so the skull balances on top of an upright spine
Towards the back, so the skull hangs forward from a horizontal spine
On the side, so the head can turn further to watch for predators
questions.explanation: The foramen magnum is where the spinal cord passes into the skull. In bipedal humans it lies centrally under the skull, which balances on the vertical spine. In quadrupedal apes it is further back.

questions.stem: How does the human pelvis differ from a chimpanzee's in a way that suits bipedalism?
options: It is much smaller and lighter, so it carries less of the body's weight
It is short, broad and bowl-shaped, anchoring the walking muscles
It is long, narrow and flat, allowing the legs to swing freely beneath the trunk
It is tilted forward and fused to the ribs, keeping the trunk horizontal
questions.explanation: The short, broad human pelvis supports the abdominal organs from below and positions the hip muscles to stabilise the body on one leg during each step. The chimpanzee pelvis is long and narrow.

questions.stem: What is the role of the curves of the human spine?
options: They let the arms hang below the knees for swinging between branches
They place the body's weight over the hips and absorb shock while walking
They allow the spine to bend fully forward so the knuckles touch the ground
They keep the head positioned in front of the body for balance in trees
questions.explanation: The S-shaped human spine, with a forward curve in the lower back, brings the centre of gravity over the hips and feet and acts like a spring. Apes have a C-shaped spine suited to a forward-leaning posture.

questions.stem: In humans the femur angles inwards from the hip to the knee, while in chimpanzees it runs more straight down. What is the advantage of the human arrangement?
options: It brings the knees under the centre of gravity, so feet land near the midline
It spreads the feet wide apart, giving a broader base for knuckle-walking on all fours
It lengthens the arms relative to the legs, which helps in swinging between branches
It allows the big toe to oppose the other toes, improving grip on the ground
questions.explanation: The angled femur (carrying angle) places the knees and feet beneath the centre of gravity, so the body does not sway from side to side with each step. This is efficient for bipedal walking.

questions.stem: Which feature of the human foot is an adaptation for bipedal walking?
options: A heel that is held off the ground for walking on the toes
Arches that absorb shock and help spring off the ground
A flat sole that spreads weight evenly when climbing trunks
Long, curved toes that grip branches while the animal climbs
questions.explanation: The longitudinal and transverse arches act like springs, absorbing shock and storing energy for the next step. Apes have flatter feet with long toes suited to grasping.

questions.stem: Chimpanzees and gorillas usually move on the ground by knuckle-walking. Which form of locomotion is this?
options: Brachiation
Vertical clinging
Quadrupedalism
Bipedalism
questions.explanation: Knuckle-walking uses all four limbs, with the weight of the front of the body on the knuckles, so it is a form of quadrupedalism. These apes can stand and walk on two legs only for short distances.

questions.stem: Which skeletal features suit an ape for brachiation (arm-swinging beneath branches)?
options: Short straight fingers and a long thumb that opposes each finger
Long arms, highly mobile shoulder joints and long curved fingers
Short arms relative to legs, a bowl-shaped pelvis and arched feet
A centrally placed foramen magnum and an S-shaped spine
questions.explanation: Arm-swinging requires long arms, shoulders that allow the arm to rotate freely above the head, and hook-like fingers for gripping branches. Orangutans show these features strongly. A bowl-shaped pelvis and arched feet suit bipedalism.

questions.stem: Which great ape spends most of its life in trees and shows the strongest adaptations for climbing and arm-swinging?
options: Gorilla
Human
Chimpanzee
Orangutan
questions.explanation: Orangutans are the most arboreal great apes, with very long arms, mobile hips and shoulders and hook-like hands and feet. Gorillas and chimpanzees spend much of their time on the ground, moving by knuckle-walking.

questions.stem: Chimpanzees can walk on two legs for short distances, but they tire quickly. What best explains this?
options: Their feet have arches that store too much energy with each step
Their foramen magnum is centrally placed, so the head tips backwards
Their pelvis and legs do not keep the centre of gravity over the feet
Their arms are too short to help with balance when they stand upright
questions.explanation: Without a bowl-shaped pelvis, angled femurs and an S-shaped spine, a chimpanzee walks upright with bent hips and knees and sways from side to side, which uses much more energy. Arches and a central foramen magnum are human features.

questions.stem: How do the relative lengths of the arms and legs differ between humans and orangutans?
options: Human legs are longer than the arms; orangutan arms are much longer than the legs
Human arms are longer than the legs; orangutan legs are much longer than the arms
Human arms and legs are equal; orangutan arms and legs are also equal in length
Human legs are shorter than the arms; orangutan legs are equal to the arms
questions.explanation: Long legs increase stride length for bipedal walking. Orangutans have very long arms, suited to climbing and hanging from branches, and comparatively short legs.

questions.stem: A skeleton has long arms relative to its legs, a long narrow pelvis, a C-shaped spine and a foramen magnum set towards the back of the skull. Which form of locomotion does it most likely represent?
options: Upright walking with a fully modern foot
Quadrupedal knuckle-walking, like a gorilla
Habitual bipedal walking, like a modern human
Bipedal running, adapted for long distances
questions.explanation: A rear-set foramen magnum, C-shaped spine and long narrow pelvis indicate a body held horizontally on four limbs, and long arms support knuckle-walking. Bipeds have a central foramen magnum, S-shaped spine and broad pelvis.

questions.stem: Why do scientists value a fossil pelvis or femur highly when deciding whether an extinct species was bipedal?
options: These bones carry the DNA that is needed for radiocarbon dating
Their shape changes markedly in bipeds, as they carry the body's weight
These bones are the only parts of the skeleton that ever become fossilised
These bones show the size of the brain, which reveals how the species moved
questions.explanation: Bipedalism changes the shape of the pelvis, the angle of the femur and the knee joint because they carry the body's weight in a new way. Skulls give evidence too, through the foramen magnum, but brain size does not show locomotion.

questions.stem: What is prognathism?
options: The backward slope of the forehead behind the eyes
The bony ridge running along the top of the skull
The gap between the canine and neighbouring teeth
The forward projection of the jaws and lower face
questions.explanation: Prognathism means the face and jaws project forward beyond the line of the forehead. Great apes are strongly prognathic, while modern humans have a flat face.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the dental arcade of humans and great apes?
options: Humans have no arcade, because their teeth grow in a single straight line
Humans have a rounded, parabolic arcade; apes have a U-shaped arcade with parallel rows
Humans have a U-shaped arcade with parallel rows; apes have a rounded, parabolic arcade
Humans and apes both have a V-shaped arcade, narrowing towards the front of the jaw
questions.explanation: The human tooth row curves smoothly in a parabola. In great apes the cheek teeth form two parallel rows with the large canines at the corners, giving a U shape.

questions.stem: What is a diastema, and in which group is it typically found?
options: A gap in the tooth row that receives the large canine of the opposite jaw; found in humans
A ridge of bone on top of the skull that anchors chewing muscles; found in humans
A ridge of bone above the eye sockets that protects the eyes; found in apes
A gap in the tooth row that receives the large canine of the opposite jaw; found in apes
questions.explanation: Apes' large canines need space when the jaws close, so there is a gap (diastema) next to them in the opposite jaw. Humans have small canines and no diastema.

questions.stem: Which combination of facial features is typical of modern humans compared with great apes?
options: A projecting face, small canines, a chin and a sagittal crest
A flat face, small canines, a chin and small brow ridges
A projecting face, large canines, no chin and large brow ridges
A flat face, large canines, no chin and a sagittal crest
questions.explanation: Modern humans have little prognathism, small canines, a projecting chin and reduced brow ridges. Great apes have projecting faces, large canines, no chin and prominent brow ridges, and male gorillas have a sagittal crest.

questions.stem: Male gorillas have a bony sagittal crest along the top of the skull. What does it indicate?
options: A centrally placed foramen magnum that balances the skull on the spine
A precision grip that needs extra muscle in the head to coordinate it
Very large jaw muscles that attach to the crest for powerful chewing
A very large cerebral cortex that has pushed the top of the skull up
questions.explanation: The crest provides attachment for the temporalis muscles, which close the jaw. It is found where these muscles are very large relative to the braincase, as in male gorillas and some robust hominins.

questions.stem: Over the course of hominin evolution, the face became flatter and the teeth and jaws smaller. Which explanation is most widely supported?
options: Larger teeth were selected against because they made bipedal walking difficult
Tools, food processing and cooking reduced the need for big teeth and jaws
Smaller teeth were needed to make room for a larger cerebellum beneath the face
Hominins stopped chewing food altogether once they began walking on two legs
questions.explanation: As hominins used tools to cut and pound food, and later cooked it, food became easier to chew, and selection for large teeth and jaws relaxed. Bipedalism is not directly linked to tooth size.

questions.stem: Which feature would most strongly suggest that a fossil jaw belonged to a hominin rather than an ape?
options: Small canines and no diastema
Large canines and a diastema
Parallel rows of cheek teeth
A strongly projecting lower face
questions.explanation: Reduced canines and the absence of a diastema are hominin features. Large canines with a diastema, parallel tooth rows and strong prognathism are typical of apes.

questions.stem: A student argues that because humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor, that ancestor must have looked like a modern chimpanzee. Why is this reasoning flawed?
options: Both lineages changed after the split, so neither is the ancestor
Humans evolved directly from chimpanzees, so the ancestor must have been a human
The common ancestor lived after chimpanzees appeared, so it was a modern ape
Chimpanzees have not changed at all, so the ancestor was identical to a human
questions.explanation: After the split, both the human and chimpanzee lineages continued to evolve. The common ancestor had its own mix of features and should not be assumed to resemble either living species.

questions.stem: Which list summarises the main trends that distinguish humans from the other great apes?
options: Larger cerebral cortex, brachiation, an opposable big toe, and greater prognathism
Smaller cerebral cortex, bipedalism, longer curved fingers, and a sagittal crest
Larger cortex, bipedalism, a more mobile thumb, and smaller canines and face
Smaller cerebral cortex, quadrupedalism, a less mobile thumb, and larger canines
questions.explanation: Compared with other great apes, humans have a relatively larger cerebral cortex, habitual bipedalism, a long opposable thumb for a precision grip, and a flat face with small canines.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes apes, including humans, from most monkeys?
options: Claws on all digits rather than flat nails
No tail, and a broad chest with mobile shoulders
A long tail that is used for balance in the trees
Eyes on the sides of the head for wide vision
questions.explanation: Apes, including humans, lack a tail and have a broad, flattened chest with shoulders that allow the arms to rotate widely. Most monkeys have tails, and all primates have forward-facing eyes and nails rather than claws.

questions.stem: Orangutans spend most of their time in trees, while gorillas spend most of theirs on the ground. Which prediction about their skeletons is most reasonable?
options: Orangutans have a bowl-shaped pelvis and an S-shaped spine for walking upright
Gorillas have a centrally placed foramen magnum and arched feet for long walks
Orangutans have more mobile joints and more hook-like hands and feet
Gorillas have more mobile joints and more hook-like hands and feet
questions.explanation: Life in the trees selects for very mobile joints and grasping, hook-like hands and feet, which orangutans show. Gorillas are mainly ground-dwelling knuckle-walkers. Neither has the bipedal features of humans.
